title: Who handed you over?
hookLine: you'd be furious if someone handed your body to a stranger, so why hand your mind to anyone who insults you? (Enchiridion 28)

lines: YOUR KEYS, HANDED TO A STRANGER.
cards: You're at a bus stop when the person next to you takes your house keys out of your hand and gives them to a stranger walking past. Take care of these. You'd be on your feet, chasing the stranger down the block.
Nobody gets to hand over your keys. A different afternoon: a stranger in a comment section says something nasty about you.
For the next three hours, that stranger decides what you think about, how you feel, what you say at dinner. You handed them the keys yourself.

teach.h: YOUR BODY, HANDED TO A STRANGER?
teach.b: In section twenty-eight of the Enchiridion, Epictetus says that if someone handed your body over to whoever happened to meet you, you'd be indignant.
But you hand over your own mind to anyone you happen to meet, so that if they abuse you, it's shaken and thrown into confusion. Aren't you ashamed of that? He's blunt.
The word for mind here is gnome: your judgment, your way of thinking, the place you decide from. This differs from the insult, a little over a week ago.
That day was about the moment of sting, and a breath between the sting and the reply. This is about ownership: who is allowed into the control room? A stranger can say anything; that isn't up to you.
But whether their words get the keys, whether they sit in your mind all afternoon and steer, Epictetus thinks that part is yours to decide. Keeping the keys doesn't mean never being affected.

A cruel word will land; you're not stone. It means noticing when you've started running someone else's script: the replay in the shower, the imaginary argument on the commute, the urge to check if they've said more.
When you catch it, ask his question, a little amused at yourself: who handed you over?
Then, gently, take the keys back.
My mind is mine. There's something dignified in that. Not proud.
Just a person who knows where their own house is, and doesn't leave the door open for anyone who happens by.

how: Some Stoic practitioners notice when another person's words have taken over their thoughts, and deliberately return their attention to their own judgment.

o: a small garden spirit from old folk tales
the memory where old insults are stored
your judgment, the place you decide from

games.q: who handed you over — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says a cruel word should never affect you at all
he asks why we let anyone who abuses us take over our mind.
section twenty-eight compares handing over your body with handing over your mind
we'd be indignant at the first and do the second ourselves.
Epictetus is gentle and indirect with his students here
he's blunt: aren't you ashamed of that?

games.q: a stranger's nasty comment has been running in your head all afternoon. what does Epictetus ask?
o: who handed your mind over to them?
how can you get back at them?
games.why: you'd never let anyone hand your body to a stranger, he says; why hand over your mind to whoever abuses you?

practice: Notice who is in your mind right now besides you: someone from an argument, a voice from the news, a comment from this morning.
Picture them at the desk inside your head, steering, and don't fight them; just thank them, walk them to the door, and close it. Then take your seat again, with your own breath and your own quiet.

wordCard.voice: Gnome. The Greek word for judgment, your way of thinking, the place you decide from; you'd never hand a stranger your body, so why your judgment? Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 28: mind, judgment, way of thinking.

carryVoice: Your line: my mind is mine. A stranger can say anything; the keys stay with you. See you tomorrow.
